title: EEOC seeks dismissal of six gender-identity discrimination cases after Trump order
description_short: EEOC seeks dismissal of six gender-identity discrimination cases after Trump order
description_medium: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission moved in February 2025 to dismiss six gender-identity discrimination cases that the agency had brought, citing President Trump's executive order, the Associated Press reported. The action concerns those six EEOC cases. It does not show that all federal agencies stopped SOGI enforcement or that thousands of cases were abandoned.
description_long:
In February 2025, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission moved to dismiss six gender-identity discrimination lawsuits that the agency itself had filed, citing President Trump's executive order on sex and gender policy, the Associated Press reported. The motion was a specific action in six pending cases and reflected a change in the agency's litigation position in those matters.

The frozen record says sexual orientation and gender identity were removed from federal civil-rights enforcement generally. The cited AP report does not establish a government-wide end to enforcement, does not document thousands of abandoned cases, and does not show that every agency changed its policies in the same way. The corrected claim is limited to the six EEOC cases and the agency's motion. Broader claims about enforcement across departments, other statutes, or later outcomes in the litigation require separate agency documents and case records.

title: CBO projects 2025 reconciliation law will reduce average monthly SNAP participation by 2.4 million
description_short: CBO projects 2025 reconciliation law will reduce average monthly SNAP participation by 2.4 million
description_medium: President Trump signed the 2025 reconciliation law on July 4, 2025. CBO projects that its SNAP provisions will reduce average monthly participation by about 2.4 million people over 2025–2034. This is a projection across several provisions, not a count of people already removed from the program or an estimate attributable solely to the expanded work requirements.
description_long:
President Donald Trump signed the 2025 reconciliation law on July 4, 2025. In an August 2025 estimate, the Congressional Budget Office projected that the law's SNAP provisions would reduce average monthly participation by about 2.4 million people over 2025–2034. The projection covers multiple changes to the program, including expanded work requirements, limits on some waivers, and other eligibility or administrative provisions. CBO also estimates effects on federal spending.

The frozen claim says more than one million people lost food assistance and dates the event to May 22. The law was signed in July, and the CBO number is a future average-monthly participation estimate, not an observed count of people who had already lost benefits. The estimate should not be attributed entirely to work requirements unless a source isolates that provision's effect. A corrected description can report CBO's projected participation effect while distinguishing the law's enactment date from future policy effects and actual benefit terminations.

title: Trump tweets “Cryin’ Chuck Schumer” on May 10, 2017
description_short: Trump tweets “Cryin’ Chuck Schumer” on May 10, 2017
description_medium: On May 10, 2017, President Trump tweeted “Cryin’ Chuck Schumer” while referring to Schumer’s statement that he lacked confidence in FBI Director James Comey. The American Presidency Project archive records the date and wording. It documents this post, not the broader claim that Trump used this phrase from January or as part of a repeated fundraising strategy.
description_long: On May 10, 2017, President Donald Trump tweeted the phrase “Cryin’ Chuck Schumer” while referring to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s statement that he no longer had confidence in FBI Director James Comey. The American Presidency Project archive preserves the date and wording of the post and timestamps it at 2:42 p.m. Eastern. The tweet itself quotes Schumer’s Comey statement. This is a discrete, verifiable example of Trump using a mocking nickname in a public political exchange. The archived post supports the May 10 wording; it does not show that Trump used this particular phrase beginning in January or establish a repeated nickname strategy. The source also does not document use at rallies, a fundraising purpose, or an effect on public debate. The correction stays with this single dated post and its immediate textual context rather than using one tweet as evidence for a broader pattern.

title: Trump campaign rent at Trump Tower rose as it expanded office space
description_short: Trump campaign rent at Trump Tower rose as it expanded office space
description_medium: CBS News reported that monthly Trump campaign rent and utilities at Trump Tower rose from about $35,457 to $169,758 as the campaign expanded into additional floors. The campaign said the increase reflected more space and local market pricing. The report documents the payments and explanation, but does not establish that the rates were above market.
description_long:
During the 2016 campaign, the Trump campaign paid rent and utilities to use space at Trump Tower, a property connected to the candidate's business. CBS News reported that the monthly amount rose from about $35,457 to $169,758 as the campaign expanded its rented space from the fifth floor to additional floors. The campaign said the increase reflected the larger area and prices in the market around Trump Tower. These details document payments to a Trump-associated property and the campaign's explanation for the increase.

The frozen title says the Trump Organization charged above-market prices. The CBS report does not provide comparable rents or an independent assessment establishing that the rates exceeded market value. The increase alone cannot establish overcharging because the amount of space and lease terms changed. The narrower claim reports the rent increase, expanded office use, and the campaign's stated explanation. Assessing whether the rates were above market would require lease details and comparable commercial properties in the same area and period.

title: State Department expands online-presence review for specified visa applicants
description_short: State Department expands online-presence review for specified visa applicants
description_medium: On June 18, 2025, the State Department announced online-presence review and public social-media profile requirements for F, M, and J visa applicants. A later notice extended review to H-1B applicants and H-4 dependents. These notices cover specified visa categories; they do not establish the frozen claim of a March 2025 DHS AI system screening every traveler for political content.
description_long: On June 18, 2025, the State Department announced expanded screening for F, M, and J visa applicants, including review of online presence and an instruction to make social-media profiles public. A later department announcement extended online-presence review and the public-profile instruction to H-1B applicants and H-4 dependents. The first policy names student and exchange-visitor visa categories; the later notice names H-1B applicants and their dependents. These are policies for specified nonimmigrant visa categories announced at different times. The notices do not establish the frozen claim that DHS deployed an AI system in March 2025 to screen every traveler for political content, nor do they document universal secondary screening or device searches and copying. The corrected account identifies the agency, policy dates, and covered visa categories shown by the department’s notices. It does not infer algorithmic political scoring or border-wide coverage from the narrower visa-screening policy.

corrected_claim.description_long:
On June 18, 2025, the State Department announced expanded screening and vetting for applicants in the F, M, and J nonimmigrant visa categories, including a requirement that applicants make their social-media profiles public for review. A later State Department announcement extended online-presence review to H-1B applicants and their H-4 dependents. These are defined visa-screening policies issued by the State Department, not a universal border-screening program.

The frozen record alleges that DHS deployed an AI system in March 2025 to pre-screen all travelers, flag political content hostile to the administration, and trigger device searches. The State Department announcements do not establish those claims. They describe human vetting requirements for applicants in specified visa categories and do not document political-content scoring, universal traveler coverage, or the alleged secondary-screening outcomes. The corrected claim should remain limited to the visa categories and policy dates in the department's notices. The wider DHS allegation remains unsupported by the sources reviewed.
